name: Hana Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Highfield for the Ferrer family. It's mostly wheat, barley and oilseed rape, about nine hundred acres, and they keep a small herd of cattle on the land that's too wet to plough. I've been there two years. Right now, in autumn, it's drilling the wheat, which means sowing it, and carting straw for the cattle, and in summer it's harvest, which is twelve or fourteen hours a day on the grain trailer.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like harvest, even though it's exhausting. There's a moment at dusk when the combine's lights come on and you can smell the dust and the diesel, and you know the whole year's in that trailer. What wears me out is that I'm still not trusted on the big tractor for drilling. Mr Ferrer does it himself, and he's right to, I'd make a mess of the rows.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: No, never. I don't see the point and I don't like the idea of a computer telling me what to think. The big tractor steers itself by satellite already, and that's as much as I want. My fiancé Daniel's a joiner, and he doesn't use it either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's fine for those who want it and I'll carry on without. At church on Sunday nobody would even mention it. I'm not on social media much, apart from photos of harvest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means nothing to me. The wheat doesn't care about search engines. As long as the grain price holds, we're fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep learning from Mr Ferrer and ask if I can drill the barley this spring, under his eye. I'd keep my money as it is, in the building society and the bit of land Gran left me. Daniel and I are saving for the wedding next September, so nothing big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Nothing to worry about in this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the land your gran left you.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Twelve acres down by the brook, rented to a neighbour for grazing. It brings in a bit every year, and it's mine. I want to farm it myself one day, even if it's only twelve acres of sheep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Mr Ferrer use any of this AI stuff?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: His son Michael does, for the grain marketing, deciding when to sell. Mr Ferrer pretends not to listen and then asks him what it said. I keep out of that one.

S0.say: I'd say AI is fine for those who want it and I'll carry on without it. Nobody would mention it at church, and I only post photos of harvest online.
S0.think: I think it means nothing to me, because the wheat doesn't care about search engines. As long as the grain price holds, we're fine.
S0.do: Asks Mr Ferrer to let her drill the barley this spring under his eye. Keeps her savings and her late gran's twelve acres as they are while saving for her wedding next September.
S0.feel: Calm, with nothing to worry about.
S0.quote: Mr Ferrer pretends not to listen and then asks him what it said.
S0.fieldNote: Hana's cushion includes twelve acres from her gran, which she treats as her future rather than money. She's modest about her skills and respects Mr Ferrer's judgement. Her refusal of AI is firm and comes from not wanting to be told what to think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second one. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's wrong if young people can't get a start, but the answer is apprenticeships, not handouts. Farms used to take on a lad or a lass from the village every year. I'd say bring that back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm glad I'm already in. I had no farming background except Gran's field, and Mr Ferrer took me on because the vicar put in a word. If farms stopped hiring beginners, that word wouldn't have been enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work harder to be worth keeping, and ask to learn the drilling properly. I'd put a bit more into savings each month. If the church ran some sort of apprenticeship scheme for village kids, I'd help with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, for the young ones mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did the vicar come to put in a word?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd been helping at harvest suppers since I was fourteen, and Mr Ferrer's wife sings in the choir with my mum. That's how it works round here. People know each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if the young ones couldn't get a start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not the farmers, they have to make money. Probably the government for making it so expensive to take someone on, all the forms and rules. Let a farmer hire a youngster without a pile of paperwork and they'd do it.

S1.say: I'd say it's wrong if young people can't get a start, but the answer is apprenticeships, not handouts. Farms used to take on someone from the village every year, and I'd bring that back.
S1.think: I'm glad I'm already in, because I had no farming background and only got taken on after the vicar put in a word. In this world that word might not have been enough.
S1.do: Works harder to be worth keeping and asks to learn drilling properly. Saves a bit more each month and offers to help with any church apprenticeship scheme for village young people.
S1.feel: A bit uneasy, mostly for the young people.
S1.quote: Let a farmer hire a youngster without a pile of paperwork and they'd do it.
S1.fieldNote: Her answer to fewer beginner jobs is apprenticeships and community, and she blames government paperwork rather than farmers. The story of the vicar and the choir shows how much her place depends on local ties. Her worry is for others more than herself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people who lose office jobs should be helped to retrain, but they should also be prepared to work with their hands. There's no shame in it. I'd say farms will always need people, at least in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I don't think it touches me. But I'd wonder whether Michael Ferrer's grain marketing gets done by an assistant entirely, and then what does he do all day? He might want my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, and keep my head down. I'd ask Mr Ferrer whether there's any chance of more responsibility, so I'm not the easiest one to let go if Michael comes back to the yard. I wouldn't change anything with my money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, a little bit wary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: That's an interesting worry, Michael taking your job. Is it real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe not. He's the son, it's his farm one day. But if he's not needed in the office, he'll be out in the tractor, and there's only so much work. Family comes first, and I'd understand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think of the politicians arguing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd turn it off. They argue about everything. I'd rather they sorted out the price of diesel and fertiliser than shouted about computers.

S2.say: I'd say people losing office jobs should get help to retrain but be ready to work with their hands, because there's no shame in that. Farms will always need people in this picture.
S2.think: I don't think it touches me directly. But if an assistant does Michael Ferrer's grain marketing, he might end up wanting my job on the yard.
S2.do: Keeps her head down and asks Mr Ferrer for more responsibility so she isn't the easiest to let go. Makes no changes to her money.
S2.feel: Mostly calm, with a little wariness.
S2.quote: If he's not needed in the office, he'll be out in the tractor, and there's only so much work. Family comes first, and I'd understand.
S2.fieldNote: Her worry about the farmer's son taking her place is unusual and specific. She accepts it in advance because family comes first, which fits her traditional values. She'd rather politicians dealt with diesel and fertiliser prices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people shouldn't expect the government to fix everything, and taxes going up isn't the answer. But I'd also say it's not right if a few city people get rich while families lose everything. Families and churches would have to pull together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine. My job's physical, Daniel's a joiner, so his is too, and Gran's land would be worth more. But I'd see people at church losing jobs, and that would be hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep things simple, get married as planned and not take on a big mortgage at boom prices. I'd help with the church's food bank and maybe let a family who lost their job use Gran's field for a vegetable patch. I'd keep saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sad for the people at church. Safe for us, and grateful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at church would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mrs Hollis, who's a legal secretary, and her husband in the bank. They've got three kids. I'd want to help without making them feel like a charity case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said taxes going up isn't the answer. What is?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Work, mostly. If physical jobs are safe, then train people for them, quickly, and let farmers and builders take them on without all the red tape. Daniel's always saying he could take on two lads if the paperwork wasn't so bad.

S3.say: I'd say people shouldn't expect the government to fix everything and higher taxes aren't the answer. But it isn't right if a few city people get rich while families lose everything, so families and churches must pull together.
S3.think: Privately I'd be fine, with my physical job, Daniel's joinery and Gran's land rising in value. But seeing people at church lose their jobs would be hard.
S3.do: Marries as planned and avoids a large mortgage at boom prices. Helps the church food bank, offers a struggling family part of Gran's field for vegetables and keeps saving.
S3.feel: Sad for people at church, safe and grateful for her own household.
S3.quote: I'd want to help without making them feel like a charity case.
S3.fieldNote: Hana is torn between a free-market dislike of taxes and real concern about city winners and family losers. Her answer is work, training and less red tape, plus help through the church. Offering Gran's field to a family was a generous, specific idea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we shouldn't rush to replace people with machines just because we can. There's more to a farm than output. I'd say it at church and to anyone who'd listen, and I'd want the farmers' union to stand up for family farms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be finished at Highfield. The tractor already steers itself, and I'm the least skilled one there. If a robot can cart and drill, I'm not needed, and I'd understand Mr Ferrer's choice even though it would break my heart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't wait to be let go. I'd talk to Mr Ferrer in the first month about how long he could keep me. Then I'd look at farming Gran's twelve acres myself, sheep maybe, and doing relief work on small farms that can't afford robots. Daniel and I would put the wedding money towards fencing and stock if we had to, and have a smaller wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, and grieving a bit. Like losing something before it's gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Mr Ferrer in that first-month talk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd thank him for taking me on, first. Then I'd ask him to tell me straight, no softening. My grandfather could tell you the wheat was ready by chewing a grain. I'm still learning that, and I'd like the chance to finish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever learn to run the robots, to stay on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't think so. I'm not good with technology, and I don't want to be. I'd rather be poor on twelve acres than sit watching a screen on nine hundred.

S4.say: I'd say we shouldn't rush to replace people with machines just because we can, because a farm is more than its output. I'd want the farmers' union to stand up for family farms.
S4.think: I'd be finished at Highfield, because the tractor already steers itself and I'm the least skilled there. I'd understand Mr Ferrer's choice even though it would break my heart.
S4.do: Asks Mr Ferrer in the first month how long he can keep her. Plans to farm her gran's twelve acres with sheep and do relief work on small farms, putting wedding savings toward fencing and stock and having a smaller wedding.
S4.feel: Frightened and grieving, like losing something before it's gone.
S4.quote: My grandfather could tell you the wheat was ready by chewing a grain. I'm still learning that, and I'd like the chance to finish.
S4.fieldNote: Hana's mood jumps from uneasy to alarmed. She doesn't blame her employer and would rather move to her own small field than learn to run robots. Her readiness to trade the wedding for fencing showed how much the land means to her.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: That's all five. Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The last one, with the robots. It's the only one where I lose the work, not just watch other people lose theirs. What would help is help for young people to start small farms, cheap loans for stock and fencing, and apprenticeships on farms that keep people on, not more handouts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe faith. You didn't ask what keeps people going. For me it's church and family, and whatever happens with robots, I'd want those still standing.

headlineQuote: I'd rather be poor on twelve acres than sit watching a screen on nine hundred.
portrait: Hana is a 27-year-old junior on a grain and oilseed farm who loves harvest at dusk, is not yet trusted to drill, and never uses AI. Her cushion includes twelve acres her gran left her, which she sees as her future farm, and she's saving for her wedding to Daniel, a joiner. Her views are traditional and free-market: apprenticeships over handouts, less red tape, family and church first, and she blames paperwork more than farmers. She's calm or quietly concerned for others until the robot picture, where she expects to lose her job, refuses to learn the robots, and plans to farm her own small field instead.
biggestWorry: The robot picture, because it's the only one where she loses her own work.
whatWouldHelp: Help for young people to start small farms, cheap loans for stock and fencing, and farm apprenticeships that keep people on rather than handouts.
